title: Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21)
hookLine: the king takes a man's land through false witnesses; Elijah confronts him

lines: A KING SULKING ON HIS BED.
cards: A vineyard in Jezreel, beside the king's palace. It belongs to a man named Naboth. King Ahab wants it for a vegetable garden, and he offers what sounds fair: a better vineyard somewhere else, or its worth in money.

Naboth says no, in the King James words: "The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee." In Israel's law, family land was an inheritance, meant to stay with the family.
Ahab goes home, lies on his bed, turns his face to the wall, and won't eat.

teach.b: Queen Jezebel finds him there. Are you the king of Israel or not? Get up and eat.
I'll get you the vineyard. She does it with paperwork: letters in Ahab's name, sealed with his seal, sent to the elders of Naboth's town. Call a fast.
Seat Naboth at the head of the people. Set two worthless men opposite him to testify that he cursed God and the king. The elders do exactly what the letters say.
Naboth is taken outside the city and stoned, and word comes back: Naboth is dead. Ahab goes down to take his vineyard.
Notice how legal it all looks: a public fast, witnesses, a trial, a sentence. Only the truth is missing.
And notice how many went along, the elders, the nobles, the witnesses; the text records no one in the town saying no.
Then, as Ahab walks into his new vineyard, Elijah is waiting, sent by God with one question: "Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?"

Ahab's reply: "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" To him, the man naming the wrong is the enemy. The story doesn't end in neat justice that afternoon; Ahab humbles himself, and the punishment is delayed.
But the question has been asked out loud, to the king's face. This week brought a kingdom split, ravens, a widow's jar, fire on Carmel, bread under a broom tree, and a still small voice.
Today the prophet's job is simplest of all: to speak for one man nobody else would speak for.

how: Jews read Naboth's vineyard as part of the book of Kings, and the story is remembered as a picture of a powerful ruler abusing the courts to take what belonged to an ordinary family.

games.q: you're Naboth. the king offers a better vineyard or silver for your family land beside the palace. what do you say?
o: refuse: it's the inheritance of your fathers.
games.why: Naboth refuses: the Lord forbid it me. the king sulks, and the queen finds a crooked way to take it.

practice: Think of someone who was treated unfairly, a coworker blamed for someone else's mistake, a neighbor talked about behind their back, and notice who went along with it, maybe including you.
Then hold in mind one small, real thing that could help: a true word to the right person, a message of support, a refusal to repeat the story.

wordCard.voice: Naboth's vineyard. The family land a king wanted, taken through letters, false witnesses and a death, until a prophet named it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: hast thou killed, and also taken possession? 1 Kings 21:19.

carryVoice: Your line: hast thou killed, and taken. A wrong dressed up as proper is still a wrong. That's day seven hundred seventy.
